about.title: About RadioBeacon
about.operator.heading: Operator
about.intro.heading: What RadioBeacon is
about.intro.p1: RadioBeacon is the software that runs an experimental amateur-radio station. The station transmits automatically, on a fixed frequency, so other radio operators can listen for it and tell whether the radio path between their location and ours is currently open. Radio amateurs call a station used this way a propagation beacon.
about.intro.p2: Instead of transmitting only a station identifier, RadioBeacon also puts short public-interest bulletins on the air — civil-protection early warnings and earthquake reports. Someone who hears the beacon gets two things at once: confirmation that the signal path works, and the bulletin itself.
about.how.heading: How it works
about.how.p1: RadioBeacon watches a small number of information sources on the internet. When something new appears, it turns that notice into a short spoken announcement (or a digital text message) and plays it over the radio when the frequency is clear. Each bulletin is transmitted a few times, a set interval apart, so a listener who tunes in late still has a chance to catch it.
about.how.flow_intro: The journey of a single bulletin:
about.flow.step1_desc: RadioBeacon checks each information source on its own schedule.
about.flow.step2_desc: Every new notice is saved, with its original wording kept intact.
about.flow.step3_desc: A long notice is condensed into two or three clear sentences. This step uses AI, stays off unless the operator turns it on, and is skipped for notices that are already short.
about.flow.step4_desc: The text becomes spoken Spanish audio, or a digital packet. The station callsign and a note that this is an unofficial relay are added automatically.
about.flow.step5_desc: Nothing is transmitted while another station is using the channel.
about.flow.step6_desc: The bulletin is broadcast, and repeated a few times a set interval apart.
about.flow.logged: Every one of these steps is recorded in this console, so the operator can see exactly what was received and what went on the air.
about.pipeline.caption: A source update becomes a signal on the air. It is collected, optionally shortened by AI, then prepared — the station callsign, date and an "unofficial relay" note are filled in — and sent either as a spoken message or an AX.25 data packet, once the frequency is clear. SENAPRED, CSN and MeteoChile ship as examples; the operator can point RadioBeacon at any public web feed.
about.pipeline.aria: Animated diagram of a bulletin moving through the pipeline: sources, collect, shorten, prepare, queue, on air.
about.radio.heading: How it connects with the radio
about.radio.p1: RadioBeacon does not control the transmitter directly. It prepares a ready-to-play audio file and hands it to the station's transmitter-control software, which keys the radio and plays the clip only when the channel is idle.
about.radio.note: RadioBeacon is transmit-only. It never listens to, decodes, or records other stations — it has no receiver of any kind.
about.sources.heading: What goes on the air
about.sources.p1: Content comes from sources the operator chooses. Two are set up out of the box:
about.sources.senapred: SENAPRED early warnings — Chile's civil-protection alerts for weather, hydrological and geophysical events.
about.sources.csn: CSN earthquake reports — seismic events published by the Centro Sismológico Nacional.
about.sources.p2: The operator can add more sources — any public web feed — by describing it in this console. No programming is involved.
about.sources.disclaimer: RadioBeacon is an experimental, unofficial relay. Every alert it transmits says so, and points listeners to SENAPRED as the official source. It is not an emergency broadcast service and must not be relied on as one.
about.ai.heading: The role of AI
about.ai.p1: Artificial intelligence has one narrow job in RadioBeacon: shortening a long notice into a few complete sentences. It works from a fixed instruction that tells it to invent nothing and to leave no sentence unfinished.
about.ai.p2: AI never decides what is transmitted, never changes the station's settings or identity, and is off by default. Notices that are already short enough are never sent to it.
about.ai.p3: If the AI step fails, the operator chooses in advance what happens: use the original text, use just the headline, or transmit nothing.
about.underhood.heading: Under the hood
about.underhood.p1: The information sources are public services run by government agencies. RadioBeacon reads them through the same web interfaces the agencies' own websites use — no special access or agreement is involved. Each source is polled on its own independent timer, so a fast-moving feed and a slow one don't hold each other up.
about.underhood.p2: An unfolding emergency usually appears as a series of updates rather than one edited notice. RadioBeacon treats each update as its own bulletin and never rewrites or merges them. Anything it has already seen is ignored, so the same report is not aired twice.
about.underhood.p3: RadioBeacon never keys the radio itself. That is the job of SvxLink, the established software that controls the station's transmitter and shares the frequency courteously with other operators. RadioBeacon builds a finished audio clip and places it in a queue; SvxLink plays clips one at a time, and only after the frequency has been silent for a few seconds. A clip that has waited too long is dropped rather than sent late.
about.underhood.p4: In digital mode a bulletin goes out as a short data packet instead of speech. RadioBeacon uses Direwolf, a widely used amateur-radio packet program, to turn the text into the tones a packet receiver decodes. These packets run on an experimental frequency and never touch the public APRS network.
about.underhood.note: Aside from fetching source updates — and the optional shortening step — everything runs on the operator's own machine with no internet connection: the speech, the packet tones, the queue, and this dashboard.
about.control.heading: Safety and operator control
about.control.item1: Silent by default. A fresh install transmits nothing. The operator has to switch transmission on and fill in the station identity — callsign, location, frequency — before anything goes on the air.
about.control.item2: One kind of message at a time. The station sends either voice or digital packet, never both at once.
about.control.item3: A clear frequency comes first. Transmissions wait for the channel to be idle.
about.control.item4: Nothing piles up. A bulletin that has been waiting too long expires instead of flooding the air later.
about.control.item5: Full record. Every fetch, every shortening and every transmission is logged in this console, and any voice clip can be played back in the browser.
about.notwhat.heading: What RadioBeacon is not
about.notwhat.item1: Not an official emergency channel, and not a substitute for SENAPRED, ONEMI, or any government alerting system.
about.notwhat.item2: Not a two-way or dispatch system — it cannot receive messages or acknowledge them.
about.notwhat.item3: Not a commercial product. It is a single experimental station, run by a licensed amateur-radio operator and shared as open source.
